title: IsoEcol 2026: Sr workshop
text:
Welcome to Part 3 of our workshop, “Strontium isotope geolocation for terrestrial ecology,” held at The 14th International Conference on the Applications of Stable Isotope Techniques to Ecological Studies (ISOECOL 2026) in Hong Kong!






How to use this site



Each section of the workshop has its own page, listed in the sidebar on the left. We’ll go through them together, but you’re welcome to work at your own pace. If you get lost, use the sidebar or the search box to find the section we’re on.

title: IsoEcol 2026: Sr workshop
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of this workshop you will be able to:

Use the assignR package to estimate geographic origin
Integrate information from multiple isotopes or other informative priors
Summarize posterior probability surfaces

Before the workshop






Please set up before you arrive




Install a recent version of R.
Install RStudio Desktop.
Run the code below in the RStudio console to install the packages we’ll use.




install.packages(c("tidyverse", "assignR","raster"))

title: 2. Combining geolocation tools
text:
Dual isotope assignment
Explain the idea in a sentence or two, then show the code.

mtcars |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(mean_mpg = mean(mpg))


  









Tip



A helpful shortcut or good-practice note.


Hydrogen isoscape
Hydrogen isotopes are commonly used for geographic assignment. Spatial variation in hydrogen isotopes is largely driven by patterns of precipitation. Since this pattern is independent of strontium isotopes, the two isotopes are great complementary geolocation tools.
How does the hydrogen isoscape compare to the strontium isoscape?

#d2H_insect_isoscape <- raster::rast("")
# how does the spatial pattern compare to strontium isotopes?
#plot(d2H_insect_isoscape)

It is important to use a hydrogen isoscape that has been calibrated to the material of interest. Here, I am giving you a hydrogen isoscape that has already been calibrated to insect wings.
Preparing for dual assignment
For simplicity, we will append d2H values for each butterfly and assume the measurement uncertainty is 2 permille.

# append d2H values for each butterfly

#d2H.sd <- c()

dual assignment
